challenges.note: Never left the muster point early

hazards.prop-door-open: You wedged the machine room door open instead of letting it swing shut behind you. A door left open behind an ammonia leak is the leak's own path into the rest of the building, spreading past the one room built to contain it.
hazards.reenter-for-belongings: You're heading back in for a phone left on the bench. Nothing left inside that machine room is worth a single step back through that door once the alarm has sounded — the plan does not have an exception for a quick grab.
hazards.silence-alarm-panel: You reached to silence the alarm panel yourself. That panel is exactly what tells an arriving responder which zone still needs attention — silencing it because it's loud and inconvenient erases the one piece of information they're arriving to use.
hazards.wrong-way-approach: You're walking back toward the machine room instead of continuing to muster. Every step back toward a room you just evacuated is a step the plan already told you not to take — the muster point is the only direction that matters right now.

interrupts.alert: A coworker just behind you has turned around and is jogging back toward the machine room door, saying they forgot to shut something off.
interrupts.cue: They're heading the wrong way — get them turned back toward muster.
interrupts.missNote: They went back in before anyone stopped them. The muster roster now has a gap where their name should be, and the plan has no faster way to notice that gap than someone actually catching it before it happens.
interrupts.why: Nothing behind that door is worth turning around for once the alarm has sounded, and a coworker who doesn't hear that from you in the moment is a coworker the muster roster is about to be missing a name for.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the muster roster — get them turned back toward it instead of the machine room door.

interrupts.alert: Someone unfamiliar with the plan has wandered up near the machine room and is reaching for the alarm panel to make the noise stop.
interrupts.cue: That panel is telling responders which zone still needs them — stop them before it goes quiet.
interrupts.missNote: The panel went quiet before responders ever arrived. Whatever they find when they get there, the one signal that told them exactly where to go first is now gone.
interrupts.why: Pointing them at the posted plan instead of letting them touch that panel is what keeps the one piece of information responders are relying on intact — the alarm stops when authorized personnel clear the zone, not when somebody nearby finds it too loud.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the posted plan — point them to it and get their hand off that panel.

lateNotes.alarm-panel: This gets read once, on your way out — it does not get touched again after that.
lateNotes.machine-room-door: This gets closed behind you on your way out, not opened again once you're clear of it.

name: Ammonia Leak Alarm Response, Cold Plant

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the annunciator panel to see which zone tripped the ammonia alarm.
steps.prompt: Check the annunciator panel to see which zone tripped the ammonia alarm.
steps.title: Read the alarm annunciator
steps.why: The panel is the first fact this whole response runs on — which zone tripped tells the plan's own muster and headcount who was actually in the affected area, and it's read once, on the way out, not investigated up close.

steps.cue: Confirm the call: leave the machine room now, per the plant's own emergency plan.
steps.prompt: Confirm the call: leave the machine room now, per the plant's own emergency plan.
steps.title: Commit to evacuate, not investigate
steps.why: The plan does not ask an engineer to confirm the leak by smell, by sound or by looking for it — it asks for an immediate evacuation the moment the alarm sounds, because the alternative is one person's judgment standing in for a plan built by people who were not standing in the room when it went off.

steps.cue: Pull the door shut behind you as you leave, rather than leaving it open.

drag.missNote: Not fully shut — the door has to close behind you, not swing open again on its own.

steps.prompt: Pull the door shut behind you as you leave, rather than leaving it open.
steps.title: Close the machine room door behind you
steps.why: A door pulled shut behind you is the plant's own first layer of containment — it keeps whatever is in that room in that room for the minutes it takes a responder to actually arrive.

steps.cue: Two things along your evacuation route are worth reporting. Find them without stopping.

decoyNotes.working-detector: This detector's battery indicator reads healthy and current. Leave it.

itemNames.dead-detector: a portable gas detector with a dead battery

itemNotes.dead-detector: This portable gas detector's battery indicator is dead. A detector nobody can trust is a detector that isn't actually monitoring anything — it gets reported and swapped, not carried on believing it works.
itemNotes.unlatched-window: This machine-room window is unlatched, swinging slightly. An unlatched opening on your way past is worth reporting to whoever handles the room after you — it's one more path out of a room the door alone was supposed to seal.

steps.prompt: Two things along your evacuation route are worth reporting. Find them without stopping.
steps.title: Notice two things on your way out
steps.why: Evacuating is not the same as evacuating with your eyes closed — noticing what's wrong on the way out, without stopping to fix any of it, is what gives the responders arriving behind you a fuller picture than the alarm alone gives them.

steps.cue: Read the wind sock and commit once your route to muster is upwind of the plant.

gauge.label: WIND DIRECTION
gauge.missNote: That route reads downwind of the plant — hold for the sock to confirm an upwind path before you commit to it.

steps.prompt: Read the wind sock and commit once your route to muster is upwind of the plant.
steps.title: Check the wind indicator before mustering
steps.why: Ammonia is lighter than air and disperses with the wind, so the muster point the plan posted only does its job if you actually approach it from upwind — the sock is what confirms that before you commit to a route, not after you're already standing in the wrong spot.

steps.cue: Walk briskly on the marked route — not a run, not a stroll — the whole way to muster.
steps.holdBreakNote: Out of the steady band — settle your pace before you either fall or spend longer than you need to near the affected zone.
steps.prompt: Walk briskly on the marked route — not a run, not a stroll — the whole way to muster.
steps.title: Move to the muster point on the marked route
steps.why: A run risks a fall on a route other people are also using; a stroll leaves you and everyone behind you closer to the affected zone longer than the plan intends. A steady, brisk pace on the marked route is what the plan is actually asking for.

steps.cue: Mark yourself present on the muster point's roster board.
steps.prompt: Mark yourself present on the muster point's roster board.
steps.title: Check in at the muster roster
steps.why: A muster point only proves everyone is out once every name on the shift roster is actually accounted for — the board is what turns "I think everyone made it" into a fact somebody can act on.

steps.cue: Stay at the muster point and hold until authorized personnel give the all-clear.
steps.holdBreakNote: You left the muster point before the all-clear. Return and hold — a headcount with somebody wandering off is a headcount nobody can actually trust.
steps.prompt: Stay at the muster point and hold until authorized personnel give the all-clear.
steps.title: Hold your position at muster
steps.why: The muster point does its job only if people actually stay there — drifting off to check on the building, your car or anything else is exactly the gap that turns a clean headcount back into an unaccounted-for name.

steps.cue: Call the plant's posted emergency contact and report the zone and the headcount.
steps.prompt: Call the plant's posted emergency contact and report the zone and the headcount.
steps.title: Notify the plant's emergency dispatch
steps.why: Dispatch is the plan's own link to the responders who are actually equipped and trained to go back into that room — a call now with the zone and the headcount already in hand gets them moving with the facts, not guessing at them on arrival.

steps.cue: Turn the flagpole crank to raise the flag showing your zone has fully mustered.
steps.prompt: Turn the flagpole crank to raise the flag showing your zone has fully mustered.
steps.title: Raise the zone-mustered flag
steps.why: A raised flag is a fact a responder can see from across the lot without asking — it's the plan's own way of telling everyone arriving which zones are already accounted for and which still need a headcount taken.

steps.cue: Read the posted plan and confirm what it asks: nobody goes back in until authorized personnel say so.
steps.prompt: Read the posted plan and confirm what it asks: nobody goes back in until authorized personnel say so.
steps.title: Confirm the plan: no reentry before the all-clear
steps.why: This is the one rule the entire response depends on — everything before this step only works if it's followed by nobody deciding, on their own judgment, that it's probably fine to go check.

steps.cue: Point out the machine room entry first, then hand over the completed muster roster — in that order.

itemNames.point-entry: point out the machine room entry

steps.outOfOrderNote: Wrong order — point them to the entry first, then hand over the roster once they're already moving toward it.
steps.prompt: Point out the machine room entry first, then hand over the completed muster roster — in that order.
steps.title: Brief the responders on arrival
steps.why: A responder arriving needs to know where to go before they need the paperwork — pointing them to the entry first gets them moving toward the actual problem while the roster, handed over right behind it, tells them exactly who is already accounted for.

steps.cue: Sign the log once responders have things in hand, closing out your part of the response.
steps.prompt: Sign the log once responders have things in hand, closing out your part of the response.
steps.title: Sign the incident log
steps.why: The signature is your record of exactly what you did — read the panel, evacuated, mustered, notified — and it's the account a plant manager or an inspector reads afterward to understand how this response actually went.

tagline: The alarm read, the machine room left and sealed behind you, the muster point reached on the marked route, and nobody going back in until the plan's own all-clear
